newsitem.title: USA: Newmont offers $2 billion for Santa Fe Pacific Gold.
newsitem.headline: Newmont offers $2 billion for Santa Fe Pacific Gold.

text.p: Newmont Mining Corp. said Thursday it offered to acquire Santa Fe Pacific Gold Corp. for $2 billion in a tax-free stock swap that would create the largest gold company in North America.

Denver-based Newmont said it sent a letter to the Santa Fe board offering 0.33 share for each share of Albuquerque, N.M.-based Santa Fe Pacific Gold, one of the largest gold mining companies in North America.
Based on Newmont's Thursday closing stock price of $47.125, down 37.5 cents, the offer would be worth $15.55 a share to Sante Fe stockholders.
Santa Fe's stock was at $13.375 when trading in both issues was halted on the New York Stock Exchange pending the proposed merger announcement. It jumped $3 to $14.875.
"The combination of Newmont and Santa Fe Pacific would be a win-win proposition for the stockholders of both companies," Newmont Chairman Ron Cambre said in a statement.
"In a consolidating industry, we would be the largest and potentially the most efficient gold producer in North America with substantial additional growth potential."

The combined company also would have the most extensive gold operations, land position and exploration prospects in Nevada and would be one of the best capitalised and most geographically diversified mining companies in the world, Cambre said.
He said the merger would boost cash flow and earnings per share after a year.
In a brief statement, Santa Fe "acknowledged receipt of a proposal from Newmont Mining Corp. reflecting the terms publicly announced by Newmont Mining.
"There is no further comment at the present time," it added.
Santa Fe also pointed out it is one of the largest gold mining companies in North America with mines in Nevada and California and exploration offices and projects worldwide.

In a conference call with investors and analysts, Cambre said the company has not ruled out any options regarding its unsolicited bid, and said he was willing to discuss a friendly deal with Santa Fe.
Cambre declined to say if the companies were in earlier merger negotiations, or if Newmont was prepared to raise its offer if Santa Fe agreed to negotiate a transaction.
Cambre said part of the rationale for the deal was that the companies' global operations were almost "mirror images" of each other, except for Newmont's Indonesia operation.
A combination would lead to savings in exploration, general and adminstrative expenses, he said.

Specifically, Newmont and Santa Fe operations would complement each other in Central Asia, particularly in Uzbekistan; South America with a combination of Newmont's Peru operations with Santa Fe's work in Brazil; and most significantly -- Nevada.
Merger-related savings in Nevada would start at $40 million per year, he said, noting there was "potential for significant savings" in the expected overlap of employees working in the state.
Newmont has about 2,200 to 2,300 Nevada employees, while Santa Fe has about 1,300 to 1,500, he said.
